objectives: Classify real numbers as natural, whole, integer, rational, or irrational.

explanation.intro: Precalculus assumes fluency with the algebra you met in high school. This topic compresses the essentials from OpenStax §1.1 so you have a solid launch pad.

sections.heading: Real numbers
sections.body: The real numbers are all the numbers on a number line. They split into rational numbers (ratios of integers, like 3/4 and -2) and irrational numbers (like √2 and π).
bullets: Natural: 1, 2, 3, …
Rational: a/b with integer a, b ≠ 0
Irrational: cannot be written as a/b

sections.heading: Order of operations
sections.body: Evaluate in this order: parentheses, exponents, multiplication/division (left to right), addition/subtraction (left to right). PEMDAS.
bullets: Tip: 'PEMDAS' is a checklist, not a license to ignore left-to-right.
Tip: a − b − c = a − b − c; a/b/c = a/(b·c).

sections.heading: Linear equations
sections.body: A linear equation in x is of the form ax + b = c with a ≠ 0. Solve by isolating x: subtract b from both sides, then divide by a.

Check by substituting the solution back in.

prerequisites.title: Exponents & Scientific Notation
prerequisites.summary: Exponent rules, integer and rational exponents, scientific notation. From OpenStax §1.2.

objectives: Apply the product, quotient, and power rules for exponents.

explanation.intro: Exponent rules are the silent engine behind nearly every precalculus formula. OpenStax §1.2 walks through them in order of difficulty.

sections.heading: Product & quotient rules
sections.body: When multiplying powers with the same base, add exponents: aᵐ·aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ. When dividing, subtract: aᵐ/aⁿ = aᵐ⁻ⁿ.
bullets: These only work when the bases are the same.
Examples: 2³·2⁴ = 2⁷ = 128, 5⁶/5² = 5⁴ = 625.

sections.heading: Power rules
sections.body: (aᵐ)ⁿ = aᵐⁿ. (ab)ⁿ = aⁿbⁿ. (a/b)ⁿ = aⁿ/bⁿ.
bullets: Distribute a power to every factor inside.
(2x³)⁴ = 2⁴x¹² = 16x¹².

sections.heading: Zero & negative exponents
sections.body: a⁰ = 1 (for a ≠ 0). a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ. Negative exponents flip the factor to the reciprocal.
bullets: Tip: rewrite 1/x⁻³ as x³, not 1/x³.

sections.heading: Scientific notation
sections.body: A number in scientific notation has the form a × 10ⁿ with 1 ≤ |a| < 10. The exponent n is the number of places the decimal moved.

objectives: Add, subtract, and multiply polynomials.

explanation.intro: Polynomials are the building blocks of nearly every function you'll meet. From OpenStax §§1.4–1.5.

sections.heading: Multiplying polynomials
sections.body: Distribute every term of one factor across every term of the other. For (a + b)(c + d) you get ac + ad + bc + bd — FOIL when both factors are binomials.
bullets: Power rule shortcut: (x + y)² = x² + 2xy + y².

sections.heading: Factoring techniques
sections.body: Try these in order: GCF, then difference of squares, then trinomial, then grouping.
bullets: Difference of squares: a² − b² = (a − b)(a + b).
Perfect-square trinomial: a² + 2ab + b² = (a + b)².
Trinomial x² + bx + c: find two numbers that multiply to c and add to b.

explanation.intro: Precalculus happens on the coordinate plane. From OpenStax §§2.1–2.2.

sections.heading: Cartesian plane
sections.body: Each point is an ordered pair (x, y). x tells you horizontal position (right is positive), y tells you vertical position (up is positive).
bullets: The axes split the plane into four quadrants.

sections.heading: Slope
sections.body: Slope = rise/run = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁). It's the rate at which y changes as x increases by 1.
bullets: Positive slope: line goes up to the right.
Negative slope: line goes down to the right.
Zero slope: horizontal line.
Undefined slope: vertical line.

sections.heading: Forms of a line
sections.body: Slope-intercept: y = mx + b (m = slope, b = y-intercept). Point-slope: y − y₁ = m(x − x₁). Standard: Ax + By = C.
bullets: Use point-slope when you know one point and the slope.
Convert to slope-intercept to read m and b easily.

topics.title: Conic Sections: Circles, Ellipses, Parabolas, Hyperbolas
topics.summary: Identify and graph the four conic sections by their algebraic form. Master the standard equations, foci, vertices, and eccentricity. From OpenStax §§12.1–12.4.

objectives: Classify a conic by its algebraic form.

explanation.intro: A conic section is the curve formed by intersecting a plane with a double cone. Four types: circle, ellipse, parabola, hyperbola.

sections.heading: Circles
sections.body: A circle is the set of points equidistant from a center. Standard: (x − h)² + (y − k)² = r².

sections.heading: Ellipses
sections.body: An ellipse is the set of points where the sum of distances to two foci is constant. Standard: x²/a² + y²/b² = 1. Eccentricity 0 < e < 1.

sections.heading: Parabolas
sections.body: A parabola is the set of points equidistant from a focus and a directrix. Standard: y = ax². Eccentricity e = 1.

sections.heading: Hyperbolas
sections.body: A hyperbola is the set of points where the absolute difference of distances to two foci is constant. Standard: x²/a² − y²/b² = 1. Eccentricity e > 1.

sections.heading: Eccentricity
sections.body: Eccentricity e is the unifying measure. e = 0: circle. 0 < e < 1: ellipse. e = 1: parabola. e > 1: hyperbola.

topics.title: Sequences and Series
topics.summary: Arithmetic and geometric sequences, partial sums, and an introduction to the Fibonacci sequence. From OpenStax §§13.1–13.3.

objectives: Identify arithmetic vs. geometric sequences.
Use formulas for the nth term and partial sum.
Recognize when a series converges.

explanation.intro: A sequence is an ordered list of numbers; a series is their sum. Two fundamental families: arithmetic (constant difference) and geometric (constant ratio).

sections.heading: Arithmetic sequences
sections.body: a_n = a₁ + (n−1)d, where d is the common difference.

sections.heading: Geometric sequences
sections.body: a_n = a₁ · r^(n−1), where r is the common ratio.

sections.heading: Geometric series
sections.body: S_n = a₁ · (1 − r^n)/(1 − r). For |r| < 1, infinite sum S = a₁/(1 − r).

sections.heading: Special sequences
sections.body: Fibonacci: each term is the sum of the two previous. Arithmetic and geometric are the main families you will see.
